newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's referendums flop amid apathy.
newsitem.headline: Italy's referendums flop amid apathy.

text.p: Seven national referendums held in Italy on issues ranging from hunting to privatisation flopped on Sunday when so few voters took part that the exercise was invalid, according to computer projections.

State television RAI said the Abacus institute projections estimated that only around 30 percent of voters had cast ballots. More than 50 percent of Italy's 49 million eligible voters had to participate for the process to be valid.

The turnout was the lowest ever for a referendum in Italy and only the second time that an attempt to change legislation through popular democracy had failed for lack of a quorum. The last time was in 1990, on hunting and use of pesticides.

Many politicians, while not openly opposing the exercise, had criticised the nature and number of Sunday's referendums, arguing that the issues were trivial, beyond the understanding of most voters or so technical as to be best left to parliament.
Voter fatigue after three general elections in five years, media indifference and sweltering heat that sent Italians flocking to the beaches also appeared to have contributed to the low turnout.
Six of Sunday's referendums were championed by the minority Radical Party, which accused mainstream parties in the run-up to voting of conspiring to ensure a flop.

It had wanted to set two new restrictions on the careers of magistrates, limit rights to hunting, scrap the Italian journalists' guild, make conscientious objection easier, and remove the right of the Treasury to retain a controlling "golden share" in strategic privatised industries.
The seventh referendum, proposed by some of Italy's regions, sought to abolish the Agriculture Ministry.
Radical Party leader Marco Pannella, a maverick civil rights campaigner who had initially asked Italy's Constitutional Court to approve 36 referendums, said the turnout was a defeat for democracy.
"The right to vote and the right to freedom have totally disappeared or are about to disappear," he said.
Mainstream politicians blamed Pannella himself for the fiasco, saying he had abused and devalued an important tool of direct democracy.
Several said the number of voter signatures needed to submit a request for a referendum to the Constitutional Court -- 500,000 -- should now be raised.

"It takes about two million votes to get elected to parliament. For 500,000, someone like Pannella can get the state to spend one trillion lire (on the referendums) and put out more than 40 million people," said centrist deputy Carlo Giovanardi.
"When people are asked to vote on important issues, then we'll return to a 70 or 80 percent turnout," he said.
Referendums have proved a powerful tool to force legislative change in Italy since the early 1970s.
They have allowed the people to intervene on fundamental concerns that the country's ponderous parliament either cannot or will not tackle effectively.
Key issues that have been put to referendums include divorce, abortion and, at the height of Italy's political corruption scandals in 1993, electoral reform.

"The referendum is a great institution, the maximum in democracy...but you can't use it on technical problems whose significance people don't even understand," centre-left Prime Minister Romano Prodi said before voting on Sunday.
